domain_name: Scope and reach of the Act
source: Original KaiSip notes written from the public law: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, the U.S. Code, SEC rules in 17 CFR and SEC publications, each opened on 31 Oct 2026. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Sarbanes Oxley Compliance Professionals Association (SOXCPA), the SEC or the PCAOB.
overview: Domain 1 asks who the Sarbanes-Oxley Act reaches and why it exists. It covers the crisis behind the Act, which companies count as issuers, how filer status changes the internal control duties, how foreign companies and depositary receipt programs are treated, how securities are registered and reports filed on EDGAR, and which people inside and outside a company the Act touches.
analogy: Think of a city that tightens its building code after several towers collapse. The code covers buildings open to the public, not private garden sheds. Big towers get an outside engineer's sign-off every year; small buildings still need the owner's own safety check but no outside sign-off. A foreign owner who opens a building in the city follows the same code, with a few local equivalents accepted. And one rule reaches everyone: nobody may destroy the evidence after an accident.

topics.overview: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act was Congress's answer to the corporate accounting failures of 2001 and 2002. This topic covers the crisis, the purpose the Act states for itself, how it is organized and enforced, and the common myths about what it created.
can_do: State the Act's purpose in the words of its own title
Explain how a violation of the Act or of SEC rules under it is enforced
Tell what the Act created from what already existed before 2002

subtopics.name: The Crisis Behind the Act
subtopics.definition: The Act followed the collapse of large public companies whose reported results hid their true financial condition, which shook investors' trust in corporate disclosures.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each major rule in the Act targets a failure seen in the crisis: unreliable reports, weak auditor oversight, conflicted auditors, and executives who could deny knowing what their reports said.
how_it_works: Congress passed the Act as Public Law 107-204, signed on 30 July 2002 (govinfo.gov, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 705 ordered a Comptroller General (GAO) study of how investment banks helped companies obscure their finances, naming Enron and Global Crossing (opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 704 ordered a separate SEC study of five years of enforcement actions and restatements; it names no company (opened 31 Oct 2026).
The Act answers each failure with a duty: officer certifications, internal control reports, auditor independence and an audit oversight board.
The Act protects investors by making corporate disclosures more accurate and reliable, not by guaranteeing returns.
subtopics.example: At an onboarding session for a payments company that has just listed its shares, the finance director, Ines, explains why the quarterly close now has extra sign-offs. Each sign-off traces back to a failure the Act was written to stop, such as results that hid debt. Ines asks the new accountants to read the Act's table of contents before the first close.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Read every SOX duty as a fix for a known failure: unreliable disclosure, unchecked auditors or executives who could deny responsibility. The fix tells you who must act.

exam_traps.trap: SOX was passed to punish particular executives from the 2001 and 2002 scandals.
exam_traps.why: The Act sets forward-looking rules for issuers, auditors and officers. Individual cases were pursued under existing laws; the Act names Enron only in a study mandate.

key_terms.definition: The official law number of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, signed on 30 July 2002.
Information a company makes public under the securities laws, such as annual and quarterly reports.

subtopics.name: Purpose, Structure and Enforcement
subtopics.definition: The Act's long title states its purpose: to protect investors by improving the accuracy and reliability of corporate disclosures made under the securities laws.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The purpose explains how each provision is read, and the enforcement section explains why the SEC can pursue a SOX breach with its usual securities-law tools.
how_it_works: The Act has eleven titles, from Title I (the PCAOB) to Title XI (corporate fraud accountability), per its table of contents (opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 302 sits in Title III, Corporate Responsibility; Section 404 sits in Title IV, Enhanced Financial Disclosures (table of contents, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 3(a) directs the SEC to issue the rules needed to carry out the Act.
Section 3(b) treats a violation of the Act, of SEC rules under it or of PCAOB rules as a violation of the Exchange Act.
So the same penalties and enforcement powers that apply to Exchange Act violations apply to SOX violations.
subtopics.example: A compliance analyst at an insurer, Rafael, builds a SOX training map for new managers. Rafael sorts the Act's eleven titles by who they mainly affect: audit firms (Titles I and II), the company and its officers (Titles III and IV), and criminal penalties (Titles VIII, IX and XI). The training team uses the map to assign modules by role.

review: Map each SEC rule the company follows back to its SOX section
Trace each compliance calendar item to a named owner and deadline
evidence: Compliance calendar listing SOX-based SEC rules and owners
Legal counsel memo mapping rules to the Act's sections
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel keep a current map of SOX-based SEC rules with an owner for each.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC staff and Commission bring enforcement actions for violations

subtopics.isaca_rule: SOX duties are securities-law duties: Section 3(b) treats a breach of the Act, its SEC rules or PCAOB rules like an Exchange Act violation, with the same penalties.

exam_traps.trap: SOX has its own separate enforcement agency.
exam_traps.why: The SEC writes the rules and enforces them (Section 3). The PCAOB oversees audit firms, not issuers.

key_terms.definition: The sentence at the head of a public law that states its purpose.
The Act's enforcement clause: a violation is treated as a Securities Exchange Act of 1934 violation.

subtopics.name: What the Act Did Not Create
subtopics.definition: The Act built on existing institutions: it did not create the SEC, and it lets the SEC recognize a private body's accounting standards rather than writing them itself.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam options often credit SOX with things that came earlier or come from elsewhere. Knowing the starting point stops those traps.
how_it_works: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 4, established the SEC (15 U.S.C. 78d, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 108 lets the SEC recognize as generally accepted the principles of a qualifying private standard setter.
The SEC recognized the FASB's standards under Section 108 in 2003; it had treated them as authoritative since the FASB formed in 1973 (Release No. 33-8221, opened 31 Oct 2026).
What SOX did create includes the PCAOB, to oversee the auditors of public companies.

rows.label: SEC
cells: Oversees issuers, markets and the PCAOB

subtopics.example: During a board education day at a regional bank holding company, a new director says the Act created the SEC and wrote GAAP. The corporate secretary, Mei, corrects the record: the SEC dates from 1934, and accounting standards come from the FASB. Mei adds a one-page timeline to the board's reading pack.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Credit SOX only with what it created, such as the PCAOB and the officer certifications. The SEC came from the 1934 Act; accounting standards come from a recognized standard setter.

exam_traps.trap: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act writes the accounting standards companies must follow.
exam_traps.why: Section 108 sets criteria for the SEC to recognize a private standard setter's principles; it does not write standards. The SEC recognized the FASB in 2003.

key_terms.definition: The accounting standards public companies follow in their financial statements, set in the U.S. by the FASB.
A body that writes accounting principles; Section 108 lists the criteria for SEC recognition.

topics.topic_name: Companies affected and which provisions apply
topics.overview: SOX applies to issuers, and not every provision applies to every issuer. This topic covers the Act's definition of an issuer, the SEC's filer categories, who is exempt from the auditor's internal control attestation, and the provisions that exempt some entities or reach everyone.
can_do: Decide whether a company is an issuer under the Act's definition
Place a company in its filer category from its public float, revenue and reporting history
Tell whether the auditor's attestation under Section 404(b) applies to a given filer
Name the sections Section 405 exempts registered investment companies from

subtopics.name: Who Is an Issuer
subtopics.definition: An issuer, under Section 2(a)(7), is a company with Exchange Act registered securities, one required to file Section 15(d) reports, or one with a pending registration statement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most of the Act applies to issuers, so the definition decides whether a company has SOX duties at all. It also catches companies before their shares ever trade.
how_it_works: A company is an issuer if a class of its securities is registered under Exchange Act Section 12.
It is also an issuer if it must file reports under Exchange Act Section 15(d).
A company that has filed a Securities Act registration statement that is not yet effective, and not withdrawn, is an issuer too.
Size and revenue play no part in the definition; private companies outside these three routes are not issuers.
A company whose only public securities are registered bonds is still an issuer through Section 15(d), so its CEO and CFO certify each periodic report.
subtopics.example: A family-owned furniture maker with 400 employees and no public securities asks its auditor whether it must produce a Section 404 report. The controller, Dev, checks the three routes in Section 2(a)(7) and finds none applies. Dev records the conclusion and sets a reminder to recheck it if the owners plan a public offering.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Test issuer status by the three routes in Section 2(a)(7): Section 12 registration, a Section 15(d) reporting duty, or a pending Securities Act registration statement. Size never decides it.

exam_traps.trap: A company becomes an issuer only once its shares trade on an exchange.
exam_traps.why: Filing a registration statement that is not yet effective already makes it an issuer, and Section 12(g) or 15(d) can apply without any exchange listing.

exam_traps.trap: Large private companies must comply with Section 404.
exam_traps.why: Section 404 reports belong in annual reports filed under Section 13(a) or 15(d). A private company that files none has no 404 duty.

key_terms.definition: Under Section 2(a)(7), a company with Section 12 registered securities, a Section 15(d) duty or a pending registration statement.
The disclosure document a company files under the Securities Act of 1933 before offering securities to the public.

subtopics.name: Filer Categories
subtopics.definition: Filer categories are the SEC's size classes in Rule 12b-2, based mainly on public float, that set report deadlines and whether the auditor attests to internal control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Filer status decides whether the auditor's Section 404(b) attestation applies and how fast reports are due. A wrong category means a missing attestation or a late filing.
how_it_works: An accelerated filer has a public float of $75 million or more but under $700 million (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
A large accelerated filer has a public float of $700 million or more (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Both also need 12 months of reporting and one annual report filed, and must fail the smaller reporting company revenue test (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Since 27 Apr 2020 (Release No. 34-88365), revenues under $100 million with a float under $700 million rule out accelerated status (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Float is measured on the last business day of the second fiscal quarter; status is decided at fiscal year-end.
The statuses overlap: a float of $75 million to under $250 million with revenues of $100 million or more makes a smaller reporting company that is also accelerated (Rule 12b-2).

rows.label: Public float (Rule 12b-2)
cells: Under $75 million, or revenue test met

rows.label: Auditor attests under 404(b)
cells: Yes, unless an emerging growth company
Yes, unless an emerging growth company

subtopics.example: At a medical device maker, the assistant controller, Tomas, calculates the public float as of the last business day of the second quarter and finds $410 million. Annual revenues are $260 million and the company has reported for four years. Tomas documents the accelerated filer conclusion and tells the CFO which deadlines and attestation duties follow.

review: Recompute the float from share registers and the quarter-end price
Trace the revenue figure used to audited financial statements
evidence: Float workings with non-affiliate share counts and price source
Filer status memo signed off by the CFO
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO document the filer status conclusion each fiscal year-end with the float and revenue workings.
audit_focus.decides: Management determines filer status under Rule 12b-2

subtopics.isaca_rule: Find filer status in Rule 12b-2: public float first, then the reporting history, then the revenue test. A low-revenue company can be a non-accelerated filer even with a sizable float.

exam_traps.trap: Any company with a public float above $75 million is an accelerated filer.
exam_traps.why: It also needs 12 months of reporting and one annual report, and must fail the smaller reporting company revenue test (Rule 12b-2).

exam_traps.trap: Smaller reporting companies never need the auditor's internal control attestation.
exam_traps.why: A smaller reporting company that fails the revenue test with a float of $75 million or more is also an accelerated filer, so Section 404(b) applies unless it is an emerging growth company.

key_terms.definition: The market value of common equity held by non-affiliates, measured as Rule 12b-2 directs.
Per Rule 12b-2 (opened 31 Oct 2026): float under $250 million, or revenues under $100 million with float under $700 million.

subtopics.name: Who Is Exempt from the Auditor Attestation
subtopics.definition: Non-accelerated filers and emerging growth companies owe management's internal control report but not the auditor's attestation. A newly public company's first annual report needs neither (Instruction 1 to Item 308).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Section 404(a) and 404(b) apply to different sets of companies. Mixing them up leads to either an unneeded attestation or a missing one.
how_it_works: Section 404(c), added by Dodd-Frank Section 989G(a), exempts issuers that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers from 404(b).
Section 404(b) itself, as amended by the JOBS Act, excludes emerging growth companies from the auditor attestation.
An emerging growth company has total annual gross revenues under $1.235 billion (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026); that cap took effect 20 Sep 2022 (Release No. 33-11098).
Status also ends on over $1 billion of non-convertible debt issued in three years or on becoming a large accelerated filer (Rule 12b-2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Instruction 1 to Item 308 lets a newly public company skip both reports in its first annual report.
None of these exemptions removes management's own 404(a) report once it is due.
subtopics.example: A drone maker completes its initial public offering in March. Its CFO, Bea, plans the first annual report and reads Instruction 1 to Item 308: neither management's report nor the auditor's attestation is due yet, but the report must say so. Bea starts documenting key controls now, so management can assess them for the second annual report.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Separate the two duties: management's 404(a) report applies to every reporting issuer after its first annual report; the auditor's 404(b) attestation applies only to accelerated and large accelerated filers that are not emerging growth companies.

exam_traps.trap: Non-accelerated filers are exempt from Section 404.
exam_traps.why: They are exempt only from 404(b), the auditor's attestation. Management must still assess and report on internal control under 404(a).

exam_traps.trap: Accelerated filer status always brings the auditor attestation.
exam_traps.why: An emerging growth company is excluded from 404(b) while it keeps that status, even if its float makes it an accelerated filer.

key_terms.definition: An issuer with total annual gross revenues under $1.235 billion; status ends by the fiscal year-end after its IPO's fifth anniversary (Rule 12b-2).
The Dodd-Frank exemption from the auditor attestation for issuers that are not accelerated or large accelerated filers.
Item 308's rule that a company's first annual report need not include either internal control report.

subtopics.name: Provisions That Exempt Some or Reach Everyone
subtopics.definition: A few provisions change the Act's reach: Section 405 exempts registered investment companies from three sections, and some criminal provisions apply to anyone.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scope questions turn on these edges. A fund adviser needs to know which sections do not apply, and anyone handling records needs to know which crimes apply to them.
how_it_works: Section 405 says Sections 401, 402 and 404 do not apply to an investment company registered under Section 8 of the Investment Company Act of 1940.
Section 405 names only those three sections, so other provisions can still apply to registered funds.
Section 802 added 18 U.S.C. 1519, which applies to whoever destroys or falsifies records to obstruct a federal matter.
Section 1107 added 18 U.S.C. 1513(e), which applies to whoever retaliates against a person for giving truthful information to law enforcement.
subtopics.example: The owner of a privately held freight broker fires a dispatcher who gave federal agents truthful information about a customs fraud. The broker's outside counsel, Gus, explains that 18 U.S.C. 1513(e) applies to whoever retaliates, so being a private company is no defense. Gus advises reinstating the dispatcher and preserving every related record.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Read Section 405 narrowly: registered investment companies escape Sections 401, 402 and 404 only. Criminal provisions written for 'whoever' reach any person, issuer or not.

exam_traps.trap: Registered investment companies are outside the Act entirely.
exam_traps.why: Section 405 lists only Sections 401, 402 and 404. Other provisions are not exempted by it.

key_terms.definition: A fund registered with the SEC under Section 8 of the Investment Company Act of 1940, such as a mutual fund.
The Act's exemption of registered investment companies from Sections 401, 402 and 404.

topics.overview: A company organized outside the United States can still be an issuer under the Act. This topic covers the SEC's test for a foreign private issuer, the forms such issuers use, and how the Act's duties apply to them, with the accommodations the SEC rules allow.
can_do: Apply the Rule 3b-4 test to decide whether a foreign company is a foreign private issuer
Name the annual and current report forms a foreign private issuer uses
Tell which SOX duties apply to a foreign private issuer and which accommodations the rules give

subtopics.name: The Foreign Private Issuer Test
subtopics.definition: A foreign private issuer, under Rule 3b-4(c), is a non-government foreign issuer that does not fail the test of majority U.S. ownership plus U.S. business contacts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Status decides which forms and accommodations a foreign company may use. Incorporation abroad is only the starting point; U.S. ownership and U.S. contacts can take the status away.
how_it_works: Start with a foreign issuer: a company incorporated or organized under the laws of a foreign country (Rule 3b-4(b)).
It fails the test only if more than 50% of its voting securities are held of record by U.S. residents (Rule 3b-4(c)(1), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Plus one contact test: most executive officers or directors are U.S. citizens or residents, most assets are in the U.S., or business is run mainly there.
Status is tested on the last business day of the second fiscal quarter; a new registrant tests within 30 days before filing (Rule 3b-4(d), opened 31 Oct 2026).
A failed test moves the issuer to domestic forms from the first day of its next fiscal year (Rule 3b-4(e), opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: A Dutch packaging company plans to list shares in New York. Its company secretary, Femke, finds that U.S. residents hold 35% of its voting shares, so the ownership condition fails wherever its directors live. Femke records the company's foreign private issuer status and schedules the mid-year recheck.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Apply Rule 3b-4(c) in two steps: over 50% U.S.-held voting securities, then any one U.S. contact. Both must be met to lose foreign private issuer status; one alone is not enough.

exam_traps.trap: A company incorporated outside the U.S. is always a foreign private issuer.
exam_traps.why: If over 50% of its voting securities are U.S.-held and any one U.S. contact test is met, it is not a foreign private issuer.

exam_traps.trap: A foreign company loses the status as soon as most of its shareholders are American.
exam_traps.why: Majority U.S. ownership is only the first condition; one of the three business-contact tests must also be met.

key_terms.definition: A foreign issuer, other than a foreign government, that does not meet both U.S. ownership and U.S. contact conditions in Rule 3b-4(c).
A foreign government, foreign national or company organized under a foreign country's laws (Rule 3b-4(b)).

subtopics.name: How Foreign Private Issuers Report
subtopics.definition: Foreign private issuers file an annual report on Form 20-F, or Form 40-F if an eligible Canadian issuer, and furnish home-country news on Form 6-K.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The forms differ from the domestic 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K, and some SOX duties attach only to filed annual reports. The form tells you which duties apply.
how_it_works: Form 20-F is an FPI's registration and annual report form; the annual report is due within four months of year-end (Form 20-F General Instruction A.(b), opened 31 Oct 2026).
The four-month deadline applies to fiscal years ending on or after 15 Dec 2011; it was six months before (SEC Release No. 33-8959, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Form 40-F needs Canadian incorporation, 12 months of Canadian reporting and a $75 million public float (Form 40-F General Instruction A.(2), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Form 6-K carries information the issuer makes public at home or files with a foreign exchange (Rule 13a-16).
Reports on Form 6-K are furnished, not filed, for Exchange Act Section 18 liability (Rule 13a-16(c)).

rows.label: Interim and current news
cells: Form 6-K, furnished as home-country news is released

subtopics.example: A Canadian mining company eligible for the multijurisdictional disclosure system lists its shares in New York. Its controller, Aiyana, prepares the annual report on Form 40-F rather than Form 20-F, as the SEC rules allow eligible Canadian issuers. Aiyana also maps which home-country releases must be furnished to the SEC during the year.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the form to the filer: FPIs file Form 20-F for the year and furnish Form 6-K for home-country news. A furnished 6-K is not a filed periodic report.

exam_traps.trap: Foreign private issuers file Form 10-K and Form 10-Q like domestic companies.
exam_traps.why: The forms designated for FPIs are Form 20-F (or 40-F) and Form 6-K. An FPI may choose domestic forms, but they are not its default.

key_terms.definition: The registration statement and annual report form for foreign private issuers under the Exchange Act.
The form on which a foreign private issuer furnishes information it publishes at home.
A report given to the SEC that is not deemed filed for Exchange Act Section 18 liability.

subtopics.name: SOX Duties and Accommodations for FPIs
subtopics.definition: Foreign private issuers with registered securities carry the core SOX duties, with SEC rule accommodations for annual-only evaluation and home-country boards of auditors.
subtopics.why_it_matters: FPIs are not exempt from SOX. The accommodations are narrow, so a team that assumes a broad exemption will miss certifications or internal control reports.
how_it_works: Rule 13a-14(a) requires the officer certifications in each report on Form 10-Q, 10-K, 20-F or 40-F; Form 6-K is not on that list.
Management of an FPI evaluates disclosure controls as of each fiscal year-end, not each quarter (Rule 13a-15(b)(1)).
Management's internal control assessment still applies to the FPI's annual report under Rule 13a-15(c).
Rule 10A-3(c)(3) lets an FPI's qualifying home-country board of auditors stand in for an audit committee for listing purposes.
Since 18 Mar 2026, Pub. L. 119-60 Section 8103 makes directors and officers of FPIs with Section 12 registered equity file Section 16(a) reports (see 3B1.3).
SEC orders exempt, on conditions, insiders of FPIs from listed jurisdictions with similar insider rules, such as Canada (Release Nos. 34-104931 and 34-105517, opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: A Norwegian shipping group with U.S.-registered shares plans its disclosure controls evaluation. Its CFO, Ingrid, notes that as a foreign private issuer it evaluates them as of each fiscal year-end rather than each quarter. Ingrid builds that year-end evaluation, with the CEO's participation, into the Form 20-F timetable.

review: Inspect each Form 20-F for the officer certification exhibits
Compare the home-country auditor board against each Rule 10A-3(c)(3) condition
evidence: Signed certification exhibits filed with the Form 20-F
Home-country law extract establishing the board of auditors
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel map each SOX duty to the FPI's forms and record every accommodation relied on.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO sign the certifications on each annual report

subtopics.isaca_rule: An FPI with registered securities carries the core SOX duties on its annual report. The accommodations change timing or who performs a duty; they never remove the duty itself.

exam_traps.trap: Foreign private issuers are exempt from the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
exam_traps.why: FPIs with registered securities are issuers. Their annual reports carry the certifications and the internal control report, with narrow accommodations.

key_terms.definition: A home-country body, separate from management, that oversees the independent auditor in some countries.
The exemption letting a qualifying FPI board of auditors meet the audit committee listing standards.

topics.overview: Reporting duties start with registration. This topic separates registering an offering under the Securities Act from registering a class of securities under the Exchange Act, lists the periodic and current reports that follow, and explains EDGAR, the SEC's electronic filing system.
can_do: Tell Securities Act registration of an offering from Exchange Act registration of a class
Name the provision that makes a company file periodic reports in a given scenario
Give the Form 10-K deadline for each filer category
Explain what EDGAR is and which filings must go through it

subtopics.name: Two Kinds of Registration
subtopics.definition: Securities Act registration covers an offering of securities for sale; Exchange Act registration covers a class of securities and brings periodic reporting.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The route into reporting decides when SOX duties start and when they can stop. People often treat the two registrations as one step.
how_it_works: Securities Act Section 5 makes it unlawful to sell a security unless a registration statement is in effect, absent an exemption.
Exchange Act Section 12(b) requires registration for a security to trade on a national securities exchange.
Section 12(g) registration follows once assets top $10 million and 2,000 holders of record, or 500 non-accredited, hold a class (78l(g), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 15(d) makes a company that completed a registered offering file periodic reports, even without Section 12 registration.
A 15(d) duty is suspended for any later fiscal year that starts with under 300 holders of record (78o(d), opened 31 Oct 2026); Rule 15d-6 requires a Form 15 notice.
subtopics.example: Share sales to outside investors leave a private software company with 2,100 holders of record, not counting employees who got shares under its compensation plan, and $40 million of assets at year-end. Its general counsel, Ama, notes that Section 12(g) now requires registration within 120 days. Ama briefs the board on the timetable.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask how the company entered the reporting system: exchange listing (12(b)), size and holders (12(g)) or an effective registered offering (15(d)). Each route brings periodic reports and so SOX duties.

exam_traps.trap: Only exchange-listed companies must file periodic reports.
exam_traps.why: Section 12(g) registrants and companies with a Section 15(d) duty after a registered offering must also report.

key_terms.definition: Registration of a class of securities under the Exchange Act, by exchange listing or by the 12(g) size test.
The duty to file periodic reports that follows an effective Securities Act registration statement.

subtopics.name: Periodic and Current Reports
subtopics.definition: Domestic reporting companies file annual reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and current reports on Form 8-K, on deadlines set by filer category.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SOX certifications and the internal control report ride on these reports. A filer must know which report is due, when, and which duties attach to it.
how_it_works: Form 10-K is due 60 days after year-end for large accelerated filers, 75 for accelerated filers and 90 for others (17 CFR 249.310, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Form 10-Q is due 40 days after quarter-end for large accelerated and accelerated filers and 45 for others (Form 10-Q General Instruction A.1, opened 31 Oct 2026).
No Form 10-Q is filed for the fourth quarter; the annual report covers it.
Form 8-K is due within four business days after a listed event, such as an auditor change under Item 4.01 (Form 8-K General Instruction B.1, opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: An industrial supplier that was an accelerated filer becomes a large accelerated filer at year-end. Its reporting manager, Abebe, sees that the next annual report is due 15 days sooner than before. Abebe moves the audit committee review and the officer certification sign-offs earlier in the closing calendar.

review: Compare each periodic report's filing date with its category deadline
Trace sub-certification sign-offs to the date the report was filed
evidence: EDGAR filing receipts showing acceptance dates
Reporting calendar listing each report's due date and owner
audit_focus.recommend: Have the controller and reporting team reset the closing calendar whenever filer status changes.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO certify each annual and quarterly report

subtopics.isaca_rule: Deadlines follow filer status: 60, 75 or 90 days for the 10-K and 40 or 45 days for the 10-Q, set at fiscal year-end under Rule 12b-2.

exam_traps.trap: Every public company has 90 days to file its annual report.
exam_traps.why: Ninety days applies only to filers that are neither large accelerated nor accelerated; the others have 60 or 75 days.

key_terms.definition: The annual report a domestic issuer files under Exchange Act Section 13(a) or 15(d).
The current report a domestic issuer files when specified events occur between periodic reports.

subtopics.name: EDGAR
subtopics.definition: EDGAR, the Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system, is the SEC's system for submitting filings and for the public to read them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Required SOX documents, such as annual reports with their certifications, reach the SEC and investors through EDGAR. It is a system, not a rule.
how_it_works: EDGAR is the primary system for filings under the Securities Act, the Exchange Act and other federal securities laws (SEC, About EDGAR, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Regulation S-T Rule 101 requires registration statements and Exchange Act Section 13 and 15(d) reports to be filed electronically.
Before its first filing, a filer submits Form ID, the application for EDGAR access, with a notarized document (Regulation S-T Rule 10(b), opened 31 Oct 2026).
If unexpected technical problems block a filing, Rule 201 allows paper under Form TH within one business day, with an electronic copy within six (opened 31 Oct 2026).
Public access to EDGAR is free, so investors can read a company's filings.
The SEC's EDGAR Business Office administers the system and supports filers.
subtopics.example: A newly registered biotech's paralegal, Sven, asks whether the company could mail its first quarterly report on paper. The corporate secretary points to Regulation S-T's list of mandated electronic filings. Sven submits a Form ID to apply for EDGAR access and sets up Login.gov credentials for the people who will file.
subtopics.isaca_rule: EDGAR is the SEC's filing system; Regulation S-T is the rule that requires using it. Periodic reports and registration statements go in electronically.

exam_traps.trap: EDGAR is an SEC rule that sets what an annual report must contain.
exam_traps.why: EDGAR is the filing system. Content rules come from the forms and Regulation S-K; Regulation S-T requires electronic filing.

key_terms.definition: The SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system for submitting and reading filings.
The SEC rules for electronic filing; Rule 101 lists the filings that must go through EDGAR.

topics.overview: American Depositary Receipts let U.S. investors hold shares of foreign companies. This topic explains what an ADR is, the three program levels and what each level means for the foreign company's SEC reporting and so for its SOX duties.
can_do: Explain how a depositary bank creates ADRs and what Form F-6 registers
Tell the three ADR levels apart by trading venue and capital raising
Decide whether an ADR program brings periodic reports and so SOX certifications

subtopics.name: What an ADR Is
subtopics.definition: An American Depositary Receipt is a negotiable certificate showing ownership of depositary shares that represent a foreign company's shares held by a U.S. bank.
subtopics.why_it_matters: ADRs are a common way for foreign companies to reach U.S. investors. Whether the program brings SEC reporting depends on its structure, not on the ADR itself.
how_it_works: A U.S. depositary bank issues ADRs after the foreign shares are deposited with it or its custodian (SEC investor bulletin, 2012, opened 31 Oct 2026).
A sponsored program rests on an agreement between the company and the depositary; an unsponsored one is set up without the company, often initiated by a broker-dealer.
The depositary registers the ADRs on Form F-6, open only if the company reports or relies on Rule 12g3-2(b) (17 CFR 239.36(c), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Form F-6 contains no information about the foreign company itself.
A Level 1 company exempt under Rule 12g3-2(b) keeps a foreign listing as its primary market and publishes home disclosures in English online (opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: A U.S. pension fund's analyst, Kofi, wants exposure to a Korean electronics maker. The custodian explains that a depositary bank holds the underlying shares and issues ADRs in dollars. Kofi checks whether the program is sponsored and whether the company files annual reports with the SEC before recommending the purchase.
subtopics.isaca_rule: An ADR registration on Form F-6 covers the deposit agreement, not the company. The company's SOX duties depend on its own Exchange Act reporting, which Levels 2 and 3 require.

exam_traps.trap: Registering ADRs on Form F-6 makes the foreign company file annual reports.
exam_traps.why: Form F-6 covers only the deposit terms. Annual reports come from the company's own Exchange Act reporting, which a Level 2 or 3 program requires.

key_terms.definition: A negotiable certificate showing ownership of depositary shares that represent a foreign company's deposited shares.
The U.S. bank that holds the foreign shares and issues ADRs against them.
The Securities Act form that registers ADRs; it covers the deposit agreement only.

subtopics.name: The Three ADR Levels
subtopics.definition: ADR programs fall into three levels by how far the foreign company enters U.S. markets: over-the-counter trading, exchange listing, or raising capital.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The level decides what the foreign company files with the SEC. Exam items test which level allows listing and which allows raising new capital.
how_it_works: Level 1 trades over the counter, cannot raise capital, needs only Form F-6 for the program, and is the only level that may be unsponsored.
Level 2 lists on a national securities exchange but cannot raise capital; the company registers and files annual reports on Form 20-F.
Level 3 lists and raises capital through a registered offering, such as on Form F-1 or F-3, plus annual reports on Form 20-F.
Source: SEC investor bulletin on ADRs, August 2012, opened 31 Oct 2026.

types.meaning: Over-the-counter trading only; Form F-6; no capital raising.
Exchange listing; Form 20-F reporting; no capital raising.
Exchange listing and a public offering, such as on Form F-1 or F-3, plus Form 20-F.

subtopics.example: A Spanish wind-turbine maker's CFO, Lucia, wants U.S. investors to trade its shares but has no plan to raise money there yet. The company's advisers compare an over-the-counter program with an exchange listing that would bring Form 20-F reporting. Lucia takes both options, with their reporting costs, to the board.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Level 1 trades over the counter; Level 2 adds an exchange listing and Form 20-F; only Level 3 raises new capital in the U.S.

exam_traps.trap: A Level 2 program can raise new capital because it is exchange-listed.
exam_traps.why: Level 2 establishes trading on an exchange but may not be used to raise capital; that needs a Level 3 offering.

key_terms.definition: An ADR program set up under an agreement between the foreign company and the depositary bank.
An ADR program set up without the foreign company's cooperation, often initiated by a broker-dealer through a depositary; Level 1 only.

subtopics.name: What Each Level Means for SOX
subtopics.definition: SOX duties follow the company's own Exchange Act reporting: a Level 1 company relying on Rule 12g3-2(b) files no annual report; Levels 2 and 3 require Form 20-F.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The officer certifications and the internal control report attach to annual reports. A company with no SEC annual report has nothing for those duties to attach to.
how_it_works: A Level 1 company that relies on the Rule 12g3-2(b) exemption files no Form 20-F, so no annual report carries officer certifications or an internal control report.
A company already reporting under Section 13(a) or 15(d) may also run a Level 1 program; its SOX duties come from that reporting (17 CFR 239.36(c)).
At Levels 2 and 3 the company files Form 20-F, which carries the Section 302 and 906 certifications (Rule 13a-14).
Management's internal control report starts with the second annual report; Form 20-F Item 15 Instruction 1 has the first report state the transition instead (opened 31 Oct 2026).
Whether the auditor must also attest depends on filer status and emerging growth company status, as for any issuer.
subtopics.example: A Swiss chemicals company moves its ADRs from over-the-counter trading to an exchange listing. Its head of financial reporting, Urs, briefs the CEO and CFO that each Form 20-F will now need their signed certifications. Urs also plans the internal control documentation management will need for its later assessment.

review: Confirm the ADR program level from the deposit agreement and filings
Inspect the latest annual report's exhibit index for signed certifications
evidence: EDGAR filing index showing Form F-6 and any Form 20-F filings
Deposit agreement naming the program as sponsored or unsponsored
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO reassess SOX duties whenever the company changes its ADR program level.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO sign certifications once annual reports are filed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Follow the company's own annual report, not the ADR level: no Form 20-F or other periodic report, no SOX certification or internal control report. Levels 2 and 3 require Form 20-F.

exam_traps.trap: Every ADR program brings full SOX duties for the foreign company.
exam_traps.why: A Level 1 company exempt under Rule 12g3-2(b) files no annual report, so the certifications and internal control report do not arise from the program.

key_terms.definition: An over-the-counter ADR program; Form F-6 is the only filing the program itself needs.
The Securities Act registration statement a foreign private issuer uses to offer securities, for example in a Level 3 program.

topics.overview: The Act places duties and protections on people, not only on companies. This topic covers the officers, directors and committees it names, and the employees, attorneys and other persons its provisions protect or can punish.
can_do: Name the officers who sign the certifications and repay incentive pay after a misconduct restatement
Tell which employees the whistleblower protection covers, including at consolidated subsidiaries
Identify provisions that apply to any person, not only to an issuer's officers

subtopics.name: Officers, Directors and the Audit Committee
subtopics.definition: The Act gives named duties to the CEO and CFO, senior financial officers, directors and the audit committee, each set out in a specific section.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam items often hinge on who must act. Each section names its actor, so knowing the actor finds the section.
how_it_works: The principal executive and financial officers sign the Section 302 and 906 certifications for periodic reports.
Under Section 304 the CEO and CFO repay incentive pay and stock-sale profits for 12 months after a misconduct-restated report (15 U.S.C. 7243, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 406 requires disclosure of whether a code of ethics covers the principal financial officer and the controller or principal accounting officer.
Section 301 makes the audit committee directly responsible for the auditor; Section 407 requires disclosure of whether it has a financial expert.
Section 402 bars personal loans to any director or executive officer, even through a subsidiary; other employees fall outside it (opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: A newly appointed controller at a listed retailer, Nadia, asks which SOX sections name the controller's role. The general counsel walks Nadia through the code of ethics for senior financial officers and the sub-certifications the controller gives the CFO each quarter. Nadia signs the code and files a copy with human resources.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Find the actor, then the section: CEO and CFO for 302, 906 and 304; senior financial officers for 406; the audit committee for 301 and 407.

exam_traps.trap: Only the CFO and the finance team have duties under the Act.
exam_traps.why: The CEO certifies too, directors and the audit committee have duties, and some provisions reach every employee or any person.

key_terms.definition: The CEO or person performing similar functions, who signs the officer certifications.
Under Section 406, the principal financial officer and the controller or principal accounting officer.

subtopics.name: Employees, Attorneys and Anyone Else
subtopics.definition: Beyond officers, the Act protects employees who report fraud, sets reporting duties for attorneys, and punishes any person who destroys records or retaliates against informants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These provisions reach people outside finance and outside the issuer. A warehouse worker, an outside lawyer or a contractor can be protected or liable.
how_it_works: Section 806 (18 U.S.C. 1514A) protects employees of public companies who report suspected fraud; Dodd-Frank Section 929A added consolidated subsidiaries and affiliates.
Protected reports include those to a federal agency, Congress or a supervisor; complaints go to the Secretary of Labor within 180 days (1514A(b), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 307 requires attorneys practicing before the SEC to report evidence of material violations up the ladder.
The SEC's attorney rules cover in-house and outside lawyers who advise an issuer on SEC filings; non-appearing foreign attorneys are excluded (17 CFR 205.2, opened 31 Oct 2026).
Section 802's 18 U.S.C. 1519 and Section 1107's 18 U.S.C. 1513(e) apply to whoever commits the act, not only to issuer staff.
subtopics.example: An in-house lawyer at a listed food company, Tariq, finds evidence that sales staff booked fake orders to meet quarterly targets. Under the SEC's attorney conduct rules from Section 307, Tariq reports the evidence to the chief legal officer. When nothing is done, Tariq takes it to the audit committee and records each step.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Look at the act and the protected person, not the job title. Section 806 covers any employee of a covered company, and the 'whoever' crimes reach anyone.

exam_traps.trap: Whistleblower protection under SOX covers only reports made to the SEC.
exam_traps.why: 18 U.S.C. 1514A also protects reports to Congress, a federal agency or a person with supervisory authority over the employee.

exam_traps.trap: Only officers of issuers can commit the Act's record-destruction crime.
exam_traps.why: 18 U.S.C. 1519 applies to whoever knowingly destroys or falsifies records to obstruct a federal matter.

key_terms.definition: Section 806's ban on firing, demoting or harassing an employee for lawfully reporting suspected fraud.
Section 307's duty for attorneys to report evidence of violations to senior officers, then to the board if needed.

key_terminologies.Sarbanes-Oxley Act: Public Law 107-204, signed on 30 July 2002 (govinfo.gov, opened 31 Oct 2026), to improve the accuracy and reliability of corporate disclosures.
key_terminologies.Issuer: A company with Section 12 registered securities, a Section 15(d) reporting duty or a pending registration statement.
key_terminologies.Registration statement: The Securities Act disclosure document filed before a public offering of securities.
key_terminologies.Exchange Act registration: Registration of a class of securities under Section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
key_terminologies.Periodic report: An annual or quarterly report filed under Exchange Act Section 13(a) or 15(d).
key_terminologies.Public float: The market value of common equity held by non-affiliates.
key_terminologies.Accelerated filer: An issuer with a public float of $75 million to under $700 million that meets Rule 12b-2's other conditions (opened 31 Oct 2026).
key_terminologies.Large accelerated filer: An issuer with a public float of $700 million or more that meets Rule 12b-2's other conditions (opened 31 Oct 2026).
key_terminologies.Non-accelerated filer: An issuer that is neither an accelerated nor a large accelerated filer; exempt from Section 404(b).
key_terminologies.Smaller reporting company: An issuer below Rule 12b-2's float or revenue tests, eligible for scaled disclosure.
key_terminologies.Emerging growth company: A newer issuer with revenues under $1.235 billion (Rule 12b-2, effective 20 Sep 2022 per Release No. 33-11098), excluded from the auditor's internal control attestation.
key_terminologies.Foreign private issuer: A foreign issuer that does not meet both the U.S. ownership and U.S. contact conditions of Rule 3b-4(c).
key_terminologies.Form 20-F: The annual report and registration form for foreign private issuers; the annual report is due within four months of year-end.
key_terminologies.Form 6-K: The form a foreign private issuer uses to furnish information it publishes at home.
key_terminologies.EDGAR: The SEC's electronic system for submitting filings and for public access to them.
key_terminologies.American Depositary Receipt: A certificate showing ownership of depositary shares that represent a foreign company's shares held by a U.S. bank.
key_terminologies.ADR levels: Level 1 over the counter, Level 2 exchange listing, Level 3 listing plus capital raising.
key_terminologies.Registered investment company: A fund registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940; exempt from Sections 401, 402 and 404.
key_terminologies.Whistleblower: An employee who reports suspected fraud and is protected from retaliation under Section 806.
